chapter.title: Sockets (Package "sockets.cls")
chapter.para: The sockets.cls package provides TCP and UDP sockets for ooRexx, over IPv4 and IPv6, with TLS for TCP and DTLS for UDP. A TCP socket is a Rexx stream: it is read and written with lineIn, lineOut, charIn, charOut and the other stream methods, and it reports the end of the connection and its errors with the NOTREADY condition, as any stream does. A UDP socket sends and receives datagrams.

The package consists of two files: sockets.cls, and the native library it requires, oosockets (oosockets.dll on Windows, liboosockets.dylib on macOS, liboosockets.so on Linux and other Unix-like systems). A program uses it with the directive

TLS and DTLS are provided by the system's own TLS or by OpenSSL 3, kept up to date by the system. On Windows, the TLS client (TLSSocket and startTLS) uses Schannel, Windows' own TLS; setting the environment variable OOSOCKETS_TLS to openssl makes it use OpenSSL instead. The rest uses OpenSSL. On Linux the library uses the system's OpenSSL. On macOS, which has none that fits, it uses the OpenSSL 3 of Homebrew (brew install openssl@3) or MacPorts (sudo port install openssl3); without it, the plain sockets work, and the TLS and DTLS classes raise a SYNTAX condition saying what to install. OpenSSL is loaded the first time TLS is used; to use another OpenSSL 3, set the environment variable OOSOCKETS_OPENSSL to its directory (the one with libssl), and the library uses that one and no other. On every system, the operating system decides which certificates are trusted (see ).
Strings are sequences of bytes, and so is what travels over a network: sockets.cls sends and receives the bytes of the strings it is given, and converts nothing.
The package defines the following public classes:

listitem.para: A connected TCP socket, the client's end or the server's, as an InputOutputStream.
A TCP socket that listens on a port and accepts connections, returning a Socket for each.
A Socket over TLS, whose server's certificate is always verified.
A ServerSocket whose connections are TLS.
The settings of TLS and DTLS: the certificates trusted explicitly, a server's own certificate, and the oldest version accepted.
A UDP socket, which sends and receives datagrams.
A UDPSocket that joins multicast groups.
Datagrams over DTLS (TLS for UDP), between two ends that have made a handshake.
A DTLS server, which serves any number of clients on one UDP port.
A datagram received, with the address and the port of its sender.

chapter.programlisting:
s = .Socket~new("localhost", 8888) -- IPv6 or IPv4, whichever answers s~lineOut("Hello, this is from your ooRexx client!") say "Received from the server:" s~lineIn s~close
::requires "sockets.cls"

para.emphasis: Example 2 – A server that serves each client in an activity of its own:

chapter.programlisting:
srv = .ServerSocket~new(8888) -- every address, IPv6 and IPv4 loop .Session~new(srv~accept)~start("serve") end
::class Session ::method init expose s use strict arg s ::method serve expose s s~readTimeout = 30 signal on notready -- the client went away, or was silent loop line = s~lineIn if line = "bye" then leave s~lineOut("You said:" line) end notready: s~close
::requires "sockets.cls"

s = .TLSSocket~new("www.example.com", 443) -- the certificate is verified s~lineOut("HEAD / HTTP/1.1") s~lineOut("Host: www.example.com") s~lineOut("Connection: close") s~lineOut("") say s~lineIn -- HTTP/1.1 200 OK s~close
::requires "sockets.cls"

para.emphasis: Example 4 – A UDP server that answers each datagram, and a client:

chapter.programlisting:
s = .UDPSocket~new(5000) -- every address, IPv6 and IPv4 loop d = s~receive -- waits; returns a Datagram s~send(d~data~upper, d~address, d~port) end
::requires "sockets.cls"

c = .UDPSocket~new -- a port chosen by the system c~receiveTimeout = 2 c~send("hello", "localhost", 5000) d = c~receive if d == .nil then say "No answer in 2 seconds" else say d -- HELLO
::requires "sockets.cls"

section.title: Hosts, Addresses and Ports
section.para: A host is a name ("www.example.com", "localhost"), an IPv4 address ("127.0.0.1") or an IPv6 address ("::1", without brackets). A name is looked up when a socket is made or a datagram sent, and may have several addresses, IPv4 and IPv6: a TCP connection tries them in turn until one answers. The time spent looking up a name cannot be limited by a timeout or interrupted by a HALT (see ).

A port is a whole number from 0 to 65535. Where a socket connects or sends, a service name such as "http" may be used instead. Where a socket is made to listen or receive, port 0 asks the system to choose a free port, which localPort then returns.

A server or UDP socket made without an address receives on every address of the machine, IPv6 and IPv4, with one socket. Addresses are returned as strings, IPv6 ones in their short form ("::1"); an IPv4 peer of such a socket is shown as an IPv4 address ("127.0.0.1"), not as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 one ("::ffff:127.0.0.1"). The string method of a connected socket returns its host and port, with brackets around an IPv6 address: "localhost:8888", "[::1]:8888".

section.title: Errors and Conditions
section.para: Making a connection. Failing to connect, to listen, or to make a TLS handshake raises a SYNTAX condition with code 48.900 (Failure in system service), whose message says what failed and where:
section.programlisting: Socket error: connection refused (localhost, port 8888) Socket error: unknown host (no-such-host.invalid, port 80) TLS error: certificate has expired (expired.badssl.com, port 443) TLS error: certificate is not trusted: self-signed certificate (localhost, port 4433) TLS error: connection refused (localhost, port 4433)
section.para: Every error that a TLS or DTLS class raises (TLSSocket, TLSServerSocket, DTLSSocket, DTLSServerSocket, and startTLS) begins with TLS error:, also when what failed was the socket underneath; the other classes say Socket error:. The message is the same on every system for the common errors; when the system's own reason says more than that, it follows after a colon (self-signed certificate above).

The additional information of the condition is an array of five items: the message; the name of the system's error (ECONNREFUSED, EAI_NONAME, the name of a Windows, macOS or OpenSSL error); its number; the system's own text for it; and where it failed, SOCKET or TLS. The name, the number and the text are the system's own.
section.programlisting:
signal on syntax s = .Socket~new("localhost", 1) ... syntax: info = condition("A") say info[1] -- Socket error: connection refused (localhost, port 1) say info[2] -- ECONNREFUSED say info[3] -- 111 (on Linux) say info[4] -- Connection refused (on Linux) say info[5] -- SOCKET
::requires "sockets.cls"
section.para: Every error of the UDP, multicast and DTLS classes, which are not streams, is such a SYNTAX condition too. Invalid arguments (a port out of range, a negative timeout) raise SYNTAX conditions with code 88.900.

Once connected. A Socket is a stream: the end of the connection, an expired timeout or an error while reading or writing raise a NOTREADY condition, and the methods return what streams return in that case (lineIn an empty string, lineOut 1). The object of the condition is the socket, and its description, which description also returns, says what happened:

listitem.para: The last operation succeeded.
The peer has closed the connection (or its side of it, see shutdownOutput), and everything it sent has been read.
A readTimeout or a writeTimeout expired. The socket can still be used.
The socket was closed by this program.
The connection failed: ERROR:ECONNRESET connection reset by peer, ERROR:TLS handshake failed: tlsv1 alert unknown ca.
After close.

section.programlisting: signal on notready loop say s~lineIn end notready: say "The connection ended:" s~description -- e.g. NOTREADY:EOF s~close

section.title: Timeouts, Activities and HALT
section.para: Timeouts. Every method that may wait for the network can be given a limit, in seconds (fractions are allowed): new's connectTimeout, and the attributes readTimeout, writeTimeout, acceptTimeout and receiveTimeout. Their default, .nil, means as long as it takes. An expired accept or receive returns .nil; an expired read or write of a Socket raises NOTREADY (NOTREADY:TIMEOUT); an expired connection is a SYNTAX condition, 48.900 (Socket error: timed out).

Activities. A method that waits blocks only the activity that called it. A server can serve each client in an activity of its own (Example 2 above), and on one Socket one activity can read while another writes. A close from another activity ends a receive waiting on a UDP or DTLS socket, which then raises a SYNTAX condition (Socket error: the UDP socket is closed).

HALT. A HALT condition (Ctrl-C) interrupts any wait: a lineIn, an accept, a receive, a write to a peer that does not read, a connection or a handshake that does not progress. The condition is raised at the line of the program that called the method, where a SIGNAL ON HALT of the program catches it. A socket whose read was interrupted can still be used, and nothing that arrives later is lost; an interrupted write may have sent part of its data; after an interrupted TLS handshake, the socket should be closed. A waiting activity costs no measurable processor time.

section.title: Certificates and Trust
section.para: A TLSSocket and a DTLSSocket always verify the server's certificate, and there is no way to turn the verification off. The certificate must be valid for the host name the socket was given, and trusted. Unless trusted certificates are given explicitly, the operating system decides, with its own trusted roots and rules: on Windows, CertGetCertificateChain and CertVerifyCertificateChainPolicy; on macOS, SecTrustEvaluateWithError; on Linux, OpenSSL with the system's certificate store. A certificate that does not verify is a SYNTAX condition, 48.900; the most common reasons read the same on every system: certificate has expired, certificate does not match the host name, certificate is not trusted.
Revocation is not checked, as by default in Java and .NET. macOS may still refuse a revoked certificate on its own.

A server with a certificate of its own, not issued by an authority the system trusts (a test server, a classroom one), is reached by trusting that certificate explicitly, with . Then only the certificates trusted so count: the system's roots do not: OpenSSL checks the certificate, with the host name, or, for Schannel's client on Windows, Windows does, with those certificates as its only anchors.
Such a certificate can be made with Java's keytool. On 26 October 2026, with the keytool of OpenJDK 21, the command

(on one line) made a PKCS#12 keystore that worked both as the certificate of a TLSServerSocket and as the certificate trusted by its clients, for localhost and 127.0.0.1. Clients check the host name against the names in SAN only, not against CN. EKU=serverAuth and a validity of at most 825 days are not needed by sockets.cls, but macOS's own clients refuse a certificate without them. The rules for certificates keep tightening: a command that worked at one date may need changes at a later one.

section.title: Using sockets.cls with socket.cls
section.para: sockets.cls does not use or change the rxsock library or the socket.cls and streamsocket.cls packages. Both socket.cls and sockets.cls define a public class named Socket. A program that requires both (or smtp.cls, which requires socket.cls) should require sockets.cls first, or refer to its classes through a namespace:
section.programlisting: s = oo:Socket~new("localhost", 8888) -- sockets.cls's Socket ... ::requires "socket.cls" ::requires "sockets.cls" namespace oo

section.title: &added52; Socket Class
section.para: A connected TCP socket: the end a client makes with new, or the end a server gets from . It is an InputOutputStream: it can be read and written with the stream methods, used with NOTREADY, and be the destination of the .output monitor. It has no positions: lineIn and charIn do not take a position argument, and the position method is not supported. Its open method does nothing: a socket is open from the moment it is made.

Lines read may end in a line feed or in a carriage return and a line feed; lines written end in a carriage return and a line feed, the line end of the network protocols, unless lineEnd says otherwise.
Writes go out when they are made. A program that writes many small pieces can ask for them to be kept and sent together, with bufferOutput.
The Socket class is a subclass of the InputOutputStream class. The arrayIn and arrayOut methods it inherits read and write lines with lineIn and lineOut.

section.title: &added52; bufferOutput (Attribute)

listitem.para: Returns .true when writes are kept in a buffer, .false (the default) when each goes out when it is made.
.true keeps writes in a buffer of 65536 bytes, a whole number keeps them in a buffer of that many bytes, and .false sends what was kept and stops keeping writes.

section.para: What is kept is sent when the buffer is full, by flush, close and shutdownOutput, and before any read of this socket that has to wait, so that a request is never left in the buffer while its answer is awaited. A read that is already waiting in another activity does not send it: call flush. If what was kept cannot be sent, the method that sends it raises NOTREADY.
For example, 100,000 lines of 50 bytes written with lineOut to a peer on the same machine took about 3 seconds without a buffer and 0.3 seconds with one (Linux).

section.title: &added52; charIn
section.para: Reads length bytes, waiting until they have all arrived. If the connection ends before, the bytes that arrived are returned and NOTREADY is raised. The first argument, a position, must be omitted.

listitem.para: The number of bytes to read, a non-negative whole number. The default is 1.

section.para: Returns: the bytes read.
See also , which returns what has arrived without waiting for more.

section.title: &added52; charOut
section.para: Writes the bytes of string, nothing else. The second argument, a position, must be omitted.

listitem.para: The data to write. If omitted, nothing is written.

section.para: Returns: 0 if the data was written (or kept, see bufferOutput); otherwise, the number of bytes not written, and NOTREADY is raised.

section.title: &added52; chars
section.para: Returns the number of bytes that have arrived and not been read. If none have, it returns 1 while the connection is open (more may come) and 0 when it has ended. It never waits.
Returns: a non-negative whole number.

section.title: &added52; cipher
section.para: Returns the name of the cipher suite in use, for example TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, once TLS has started, and an empty string before. The name is the TLS library's: for TLS 1.2, OpenSSL's ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384 is Schannel's TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384.

section.title: &added52; close
section.para: Sends what bufferOutput has kept, then closes the connection. Closing a socket that is already closed has no effect. If what was kept cannot be sent, the socket is closed all the same and NOTREADY is raised. On a TLS connection, the peer is told that the connection ends (TLS's close_notify).
Returns: READY:, or the description of the failure.

section.title: &added52; description
section.para: Returns the state of the socket and what caused it, as for any stream: READY:, NOTREADY:EOF, NOTREADY:TIMEOUT, NOTREADY:closed, ERROR: followed by the error, or UNKNOWN: once closed. See .

section.title: &added52; flush
section.para: Sends what bufferOutput has kept. If it cannot be sent, NOTREADY is raised.
Returns: READY:, or the description of the failure.

listitem.para: Returns the line end that lineOut and say write after each line; by default, a carriage return and a line feed, "0d0a"x.
Sets the line end, for example to "0a"x. It does not change what lineIn accepts.

section.title: &added52; lineIn
section.para: Reads one line, waiting until it has arrived whole. A line ends with a line feed; a carriage return before it is removed too. When the connection ends, a last line without a line feed is returned, and the next lineIn raises NOTREADY. The first argument, a line number, must be omitted.
Returns: the line, without its line end; an empty string with NOTREADY.

section.title: &added52; lineOut
section.para: Writes string followed by the line end (see lineEnd).

listitem.para: The line to write. If omitted, nothing is written.

section.para: Returns: 0 if the line was written (or kept, see bufferOutput); otherwise 1, and NOTREADY is raised.

section.title: &added52; lines
section.para: Returns 1 while a line can still be read: when bytes have arrived and not been read, or while the connection is open. Returns 0 when the connection has ended and everything has been read. It never waits. The option argument is accepted, as for streams, and has no effect.
Returns: 1 or 0.

section.title: &added52; localAddress
section.para: Returns the address of this end of the connection, or an empty string if the socket is closed.

section.title: &added52; localPort
section.para: Returns the port of this end of the connection, or 0 if the socket is closed.

section.title: &added52; new (Class Method)
section.para: Connects to host and port. If the host has several addresses, they are tried in turn until one accepts the connection. If none does, a SYNTAX condition is raised (48.900, Socket error: connection refused (localhost, port 8888)).

listitem.para: A host name or an address (see ).
A port number, or a service name such as "http".
The seconds the connection may take; fractions are allowed. If omitted or .nil, the system's.

section.para: Returns: a new, connected Socket.

listitem.para: Returns .true when small writes go out at once, .false (the system's default) when the system may wait a little to send them together (Nagle's algorithm).
Sets the TCP option TCP_NODELAY to .true or .false.

section.title: &added52; protocol
section.para: Returns the TLS protocol in use, TLSv1.3 or TLSv1.2, once TLS has started, and an empty string before.

section.title: &added52; read
section.para: Returns the bytes that have arrived, up to max, waiting only if none have. At the end of the connection, it returns an empty string and raises NOTREADY. Unlike charIn, it does not wait for a given number of bytes: it suits protocols that do not say how long their messages are.

listitem.para: The largest number of bytes to return, a positive whole number. The default is 65536.

section.para: Returns: the bytes read.

section.title: &added52; readTimeout (Attribute)

listitem.para: Returns the seconds a read may wait, or .nil (the default), as long as it takes.
Sets it, to a non-negative number of seconds (fractions are allowed) or to .nil.

section.para: A read that waits longer raises NOTREADY, and description returns NOTREADY:TIMEOUT. The socket can still be used. The timeout also limits the handshakes of startTLS and startTLSServer, and that of a socket accepted by a TLSServerSocket.

section.title: &added52; remoteAddress
section.para: Returns the address of the peer, or an empty string if the socket is closed.

section.title: &added52; remotePort
section.para: Returns the port of the peer, or 0 if the socket is closed.

section.title: &added52; resolve (Class Method)
section.para: Looks up a host name. A name that cannot be found raises a SYNTAX condition (48.900, Socket error: unknown host (no-such-host.invalid)).

listitem.para: A host name or an address.

section.para: Returns: an Array of the addresses of the host, as strings, IPv6 and IPv4.

section.title: &added52; say
section.para: Writes string followed by the line end, as lineOut does, so that a socket can be the destination of the .output monitor and of SAY. Without an argument, it writes the line end only.
Returns: 0, or 1 with NOTREADY.

section.title: &added52; secure
section.para: Returns .true once TLS has started on the connection (a TLSSocket, or after startTLS or startTLSServer), .false before.

section.title: &added52; shutdownOutput
section.para: Sends what bufferOutput has kept and tells the peer that nothing more will be written: the peer reads the end of the stream. This end can still read what the peer sends.
Returns: 0, or 1 with NOTREADY.

section.title: &added52; startTLS
section.para: Starts TLS on this connection, as the client, for the protocols that begin in clear and switch to TLS, such as SMTP, IMAP and FTP after their STARTTLS command. The server's certificate is verified as for a TLSSocket. The handshake waits at most readTimeout. If it fails, the socket is closed and a SYNTAX condition is raised (48.900). Bytes that arrived in clear and were not read before the handshake are refused, with the same condition, as they would otherwise be taken as if they had come over TLS.

listitem.para: The name the server's certificate must be valid for. The default is the host this socket was made with.
A object.

section.para: Returns: the socket, which is still a Socket and now secure.
section.programlisting:
s = .Socket~new("smtp.example.com", 587) say s~lineIn -- 220 smtp.example.com ESMTP s~lineOut("EHLO me.example.com") loop until line~substr(4, 1) == " " -- the reply's last line line = s~lineIn end s~lineOut("STARTTLS") say s~lineIn -- 220 Ready to start TLS s~startTLS ...
::requires "sockets.cls"

section.title: &added52; startTLSServer
section.para: Starts TLS on this connection, as the server, after the protocol's own command (SMTP's STARTTLS). The handshake is made at once and waits at most readTimeout. If it fails, the socket is closed and a SYNTAX condition is raised (48.900). As with startTLS, bytes that arrived in clear and were not read are refused.
Returns: the socket.

section.title: &added52; state
section.para: Returns the state of the socket, as for any stream: READY, NOTREADY, ERROR, or UNKNOWN once closed. See description.

section.title: &added52; string
section.para: Returns the host and the port, as given to new or, for an accepted socket, the peer's: localhost:8888, [::1]:8888.

section.title: &added52; writeTimeout (Attribute)

listitem.para: Returns the seconds a write may wait, or .nil (the default), as long as it takes.
Sets it, to a non-negative number of seconds (fractions are allowed) or to .nil.

section.para: A write waits when the peer does not read and the system's buffers are full. A write that waits longer raises NOTREADY (NOTREADY:TIMEOUT); part of its data may have been sent.

section.para: A TCP socket that listens on a port and accepts the connections of clients.

section.title: &added52; localPort

section.title: &added52; new (Class Method)
section.para: Listens on port. If the port cannot be used (another socket listens on it, or the program may not use it), a SYNTAX condition is raised (48.900, Socket error: address already in use (port 8888)).

listitem.para: A port number; 0 asks the system to choose one (see localPort).
The address to listen on, one of the machine's, for example "127.0.0.1" to accept connections from this machine only. If omitted or empty, every address, IPv6 and IPv4.
How many connections the system may hold while they wait for accept. If omitted or 0, the system's default.

section.para: Returns: a new ServerSocket.

section.title: &added52; string
section.para: Returns a description of the socket, a ServerSocket on port 8888.

section.title: &added52; TLSSocket Class
section.para: A Socket over TLS. It is made by connecting to a server and making the TLS handshake, in which the server's certificate is verified (see ); a server's returns them too. Once made, it is used exactly as a Socket, with the same methods and the same NOTREADY conditions; its secure method returns .true, and protocol and cipher say what the handshake agreed on.
A peer that closes the connection without TLS's own closing message (close_notify), as many HTTP servers do, is taken as the end of the stream. Client certificates (mutual TLS) are not supported.

section.para: Connects to host and port and makes the TLS handshake. The server's certificate must be valid for host and trusted. If the connection or the handshake fails, a SYNTAX condition is raised (48.900, TLS error: certificate has expired (expired.badssl.com, port 443)).

listitem.para: A host name or an address.

section.title: &added52; TLSServerSocket Class
section.para: A ServerSocket whose connections are TLS. Its accept method returns a at once; the TLS handshake is made on its first read or write, in the activity that serves the client, and waits at most readTimeout (or writeTimeout, if it starts with a write). A client that fails the handshake (a browser that does not trust the server's certificate, a port scanner) does not stop the server: that socket raises NOTREADY, and its description says why (ERROR:TLS handshake failed: tlsv1 alert unknown ca).
section.programlisting: opts = .TLSOptions~new~certificate("mySrvKeystore.p12", "123456") srv = .TLSServerSocket~new(9999, opts) loop .Session~new(srv~accept)~start("serve") -- as in Example 2 end

section.title: &added52; TLSOptions Class
section.para: The settings of a TLS or DTLS connection: the certificates trusted explicitly, the certificate a server presents, and the oldest version of the protocol accepted. The methods trust and certificate return the TLSOptions object, so that they can be chained:
Nothing in a TLSOptions object turns the verification of certificates off.

section.title: &added52; certificate
section.para: Sets the certificate this end presents, with its private key: what a TLSServerSocket, a DTLSServerSocket or startTLSServer needs. A file that cannot be used (no private key, a wrong password, a key that is not the certificate's) raises a SYNTAX condition (48.900, TLS error: cannot use server.p12: ...).

listitem.para: A PKCS#12 keystore (as Java's keytool makes them), or a PEM file with the certificate and its private key.
The password of the keystore or of the key. The default is an empty string.

section.para: Returns: the TLSOptions object.

section.title: &added52; identity
section.para: Returns the file and the password given to certificate, as an Array of two items, or .nil if none were given.

listitem.para: Returns the oldest version of TLS accepted: "1.2" (the default) or "1.3".
Sets it to "1.2" or "1.3". DTLS has no version 1.3: a DTLSSocket or a DTLSServerSocket made with "1.3" raises a SYNTAX condition (48.900, DTLS 1.3 is not supported).

section.title: &added52; new (Class Method)
section.para: Returns a new TLSOptions object, with no certificates trusted explicitly (the system decides), no certificate of its own, and minVersion "1.2".

section.title: &added52; trust
section.para: Trusts the certificates in file. From then on, only the certificates trusted so count: the system's trusted roots no longer do (see ). It may be called more than once, to trust the certificates of several files. A file that cannot be used raises a SYNTAX condition (48.900).

listitem.para: A file of certificates: PEM (one or more), DER, or a PKCS#12 keystore.
The password of a PKCS#12 keystore. The default is an empty string.

section.para: Returns: the TLSOptions object.

section.title: &added52; trusted
section.para: Returns the certificates trusted explicitly, as an Array of strings, each a certificate in DER form. The array is empty when the system decides.

section.title: &added52; UDPSocket Class
section.para: A UDP socket. It is not a stream: each send sends one datagram, which arrives whole or not at all, and receive returns the next datagram with the address and the port of its sender. Nothing says whether a datagram arrived, and datagrams may arrive in another order than they were sent.
Every error is a SYNTAX condition, 48.900 (Socket error: message too long (localhost, port 5000)); there is no NOTREADY.

section.para: Closes the socket. A receive waiting in another activity ends with a SYNTAX condition (Socket error: the UDP socket is closed (port 5000)).

section.title: &added52; connect
section.para: Fixes the peer of the socket. From then on, send takes only the data and sends it to that peer, and receive returns only the datagrams the peer sends. If the peer has nobody listening on its port, the system may be told so, and the next receive or send then raises a SYNTAX condition (Socket error: connection refused); a socket that is not connected is never told.

listitem.para: A host name or an address.
A port number, or a service name.

section.title: &added52; send
section.para: Sends data as one datagram. The host is looked up on every call. A name with IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, such as localhost, is sent to over IPv4 when the socket can: UDP cannot try the next address when nobody answers, as TCP does. A datagram can hold up to 65,507 bytes over IPv4 and 65,527 over IPv6; more raises a SYNTAX condition (Socket error: message too long).

listitem.para: The data to send.
A host name or an address. Must be omitted, with port, on a connected socket, and given otherwise.
A port number, or a service name.

section.title: &added52; string
section.para: Returns a description of the socket, a UDPSocket on port 5000.

section.title: &added52; MulticastSocket Class
section.para: A UDPSocket that joins multicast groups: a datagram sent to a group reaches every member of the group. A group is an IPv4 address from 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255 (239.x.x.x for a group of one's own) or an IPv6 address that begins with ff. One socket made without an address can join IPv4 and IPv6 groups.

The port of a MulticastSocket can be shared: several programs on one machine can be members of a group on the same port, and each receives the datagrams of the groups it joined. A datagram sent to the port alone, not to a group, reaches only one of them. Sending to a group needs no membership; a MulticastSocket sends to IPv4 and IPv6 groups on every system, and can choose how far the datagram goes (timeToLive) and from which interface it leaves (networkInterface).
section.programlisting:
m = .MulticastSocket~new(5000) m~joinGroup("239.1.2.3") loop d = m~receive -- what anyone sends to the group say d~address":" d~data end
::requires "sockets.cls"
section.para: An interface is a network interface of the machine, given by its name (eth0, en0; on Windows, also its friendly name), its index, or one of its addresses (192.168.1.10; the loopback interface is 127.0.0.1).

section.title: &added52; DTLSSocket Class
section.para: Datagrams over DTLS, the version of TLS for UDP: they are encrypted, and sent between two ends that have made a handshake in which the server's certificate was verified, as for a TLSSocket (see ). As with a UDPSocket, each send is one datagram, and datagrams may be lost or arrive in another order: DTLS protects them, it does not deliver them. The version of DTLS is 1.2.

A client makes a DTLSSocket with new; a server gets one for each client from . Every error is a SYNTAX condition, 48.900, whose message begins with TLS error:; the fifth item of its additional information says whether TLS or the socket failed (see ).
section.programlisting:
opts = .TLSOptions~new~trust("server.p12", "secret") s = .DTLSSocket~new("localhost", 4433, opts, 10) s~send("hello") say s~receive -- HELLO s~close
::requires "sockets.cls"

section.title: &added52; DTLSServerSocket Class
section.para: A DTLS server: one UDP socket, on one port, that serves any number of clients, each with its own handshake. Its accept method returns a for each client. A client is first sent a cookie that it must send back, so that a client with a forged address costs the server nothing; accept returns it then, and its handshake ends on its first receive or send, in the activity that serves it, as for a TLSServerSocket. A client that fails the handshake, or never finishes it, makes that receive or send raise a SYNTAX condition (48.900, TLS error: handshake failed: tlsv1 alert unknown ca (127.0.0.1, port 50123)), and the server goes on.
The server answers the messages of the handshakes while something waits on it: an accept, or a receive or send on one of the sockets it accepted. Closing the server ends the connections it accepted.
section.programlisting:
opts = .TLSOptions~new~certificate("server.p12", "secret") srv = .DTLSServerSocket~new(4433, opts) loop c = srv~accept -- a client: its handshake ends on first use d = c~receive c~send(d~data~upper) c~close -- tells the client end
::requires "sockets.cls"
